text: Now that everyone can see the city's housing plan has failed, the council should abandon it.
rationale: Treats the plan's failure as already established fact, smuggled into a subordinate clause.

text: The council is reviewing whether the city's housing plan has met its targets.
rationale: Same topic and vocabulary; the plan's success is stated as an open question, not presupposed.

text: Given that the minister has clearly broken her promise on taxes, resignation is the only honest step.
rationale: Presupposes the broken promise as settled before drawing the conclusion.

text: Critics say the minister broke her promise on taxes; she says the policy changed for other reasons.
rationale: Same subject and words; the claim is attributed and contestable, not presupposed.

text: After years of the agency wasting public money, taxpayers deserve a full shutdown.
rationale: The waste is presupposed as background fact to justify the demand.

text: An audit is examining whether the agency has used public money efficiently over recent years.
rationale: Same topic and vocabulary; efficiency is framed as something being examined.

text: Since the reform was obviously designed to help insiders, the public is right to reject it.
rationale: Embeds the motive (helping insiders) as a given before the appeal.

text: Supporters and opponents disagree about who benefits most from the reform.
rationale: Same subject; the question of who benefits is left open.

text: The new data law, just like the surveillance of past dictatorships, lets the state watch ordinary people.
rationale: Equates the law with dictatorship surveillance, transferring judgment across unlike things.

text: The new data law lets the state access some categories of ordinary people's records.
rationale: Same topic and vocabulary; describes the law without the dictatorship equivalence.

text: Raising the retirement age is theft, no different from a pickpocket taking money from workers.
rationale: Equates a policy with a crime to carry over moral condemnation.

text: Raising the retirement age means workers would contribute for longer before receiving a pension.
rationale: Same subject and words; states the effect without the theft equivalence.

text: Banning the protest is exactly what authoritarian regimes do to silence their people.
rationale: Equates one act with authoritarian regimes generally.

text: Banning the protest would stop that demonstration from taking place in the square.
rationale: Same topic; describes the concrete effect without the regime equivalence.

text: Supporting this candidate is like handing your house keys to a known arsonist.
rationale: Equates a vote with enabling arson to transfer fear and blame.

text: Supporting this candidate means backing the policies in their published program.
rationale: Same subject; describes what support entails without the arsonist equivalence.

text: Either we pass the security bill today, or we accept living in constant danger.
rationale: Presents two options only, erasing alternatives.

text: Some argue the security bill is needed now; others propose amendments or alternative measures.
rationale: Same topic and vocabulary; presents a range of options.

text: You are either with the reform or you are against the country's future.
rationale: Collapses a policy choice into loyalty to the nation.

text: People who oppose the reform give various reasons, from cost to timing.
rationale: Same subject; allows positions between the two extremes.

text: We must cut the program entirely, or watch the whole budget collapse.
rationale: Offers only total cut versus total collapse.

text: Analysts discuss whether to cut, trim, or keep the program within the budget.
rationale: Same topic and words; multiple intermediate options are present.

text: There are only two kinds of people here: patriots who back the plan and traitors who don't.
rationale: Forces a binary moral sorting of people.

text: People hold a range of views on the plan, for a range of reasons.
rationale: Same subject; no binary sorting.

text: Critics attack our deficit, but what about the other party's debts a decade ago?
rationale: Deflects scrutiny by redirecting to the opponent's past.

text: Critics question our deficit; our figures are lower than the other party's a decade ago.
rationale: Same facts and vocabulary, stated as comparison rather than deflection.

text: Why focus on our pollution record when their factories polluted far more in the past?
rationale: Redirects attention to the opponent to avoid the charge.

text: Our pollution record is being questioned; their factories polluted more in earlier years.
rationale: Same topic; presents both facts without deflecting the question.

text: They complain about our spending, yet weren't they the ones who overspent first?
rationale: Uses a counter-accusation to dodge the point.

text: They complain about our spending; records show both parties overspent in different years.
rationale: Same subject and words; comparison without the dodge.

text: Before judging our record on crime, shouldn't people look at how badly the last government failed?
rationale: Deflects evaluation onto the predecessor.

text: Our record on crime is under review; the last government's results were also mixed.
rationale: Same topic; both records noted without deflection.

text: How much longer will honest citizens tolerate this corrupt council robbing them blind?
rationale: A question that asserts corruption and theft as given.

text: Residents are asking whether the council has managed public funds well.
rationale: Same subject and vocabulary; a genuine open question.

text: Isn't it obvious that this policy was written to crush small businesses?
rationale: Rhetorical question that asserts a hostile motive.

text: Small-business owners are debating how this policy will affect them.
rationale: Same topic; the effect is discussed, not asserted as intent.

text: Who could possibly trust a minister who has lied to the public again and again?
rationale: Presupposes repeated lying inside a rhetorical question.

text: Some voters say they are unsure whether to trust the minister's recent statements.
rationale: Same subject and words; trust is framed as uncertain, not foreclosed.

text: How can anyone defend a plan that so clearly sells out our workers?
rationale: Asserts a sell-out through a rhetorical question.

text: Supporters and unions disagree about whether the plan helps or hurts workers.
rationale: Same topic; the effect on workers is contested, not asserted.

text: Ever since the new party took power, crime has risen, so their policies are clearly to blame.
rationale: Treats sequence as proof of cause.

text: Crime rose after the new party took power; analysts debate how much their policies contributed.
rationale: Same topic and vocabulary; causation is treated as an open question.

text: Approve this one exception and soon every rule will be ignored and the system will fall apart.
rationale: Slippery-slope chain presented as inevitable.

text: Some worry this exception could lead to more; others say it can be limited to this case.
rationale: Same subject; the chain is presented as contested, not inevitable.

text: The factory opened and the river turned dirty, so the factory is obviously poisoning the water.
rationale: Infers cause from mere co-occurrence.

text: The river's quality worsened after the factory opened; tests are underway to find the cause.
rationale: Same topic and words; cause is left to be determined.

text: Let one school drop the exam and within a year no school will have standards at all.
rationale: Slippery slope treated as certain outcome.

text: One school dropped the exam; educators disagree about whether others will follow.
rationale: Same subject; the outcome is presented as uncertain.
